Sap
SAP
n. (the vital juice of a plant; that which sustains growth)
Hebrew saba, to be satisfied or filled to the full — the Authorized Version's full of sap renders a single word meaning well-watered, satisfied. Old English sæp, the juice of a plant.

Biblical Definition

The trees of the LORD are full of sap; the cedars of Lebanon, which he hath planted. The psalm is a long catalogue of God's works in creation, and this line is doing something specific with the cedars. They are the largest, most valuable, most sought-after timber in the ancient Near East — the trees kings imported for palaces and temples. The psalmist calls them the trees of the LORD, and adds the decisive clause: which he hath planted. Nobody planted the cedars of Lebanon. They grew where no man sowed, on mountains no man terraced, and they were full of sap — thriving, well-watered, alive — entirely apart from human cultivation. The surrounding verses keep the same emphasis: he causeth the grass to grow for the cattle, and herb for the service of man. God is portrayed as the actual gardener of the world, and the psalm shows him feeding beasts and birds that no one farms. The image of inward sap as the mark of real life carries through Scripture in the places one would expect. The blessed man of Psalm 1 shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither. Jeremiah says such a man shall not be careful in the year of drought. And the Lord names the source directly: I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): the juice of plants of any kind, which flows chiefly between the wood and the bark; the vital juice.

expand to see more

SAP, n. The juice of plants of any kind, which flows chiefly between the wood and the bark.

SAPPY, a. Abounding with sap; juicy; succulent; young; not firm; weak.

CEDAR, n. The name of different species of trees; the cedar of Lebanon is a large and durable tree, much valued for building.

HUSBANDMAN, n. A farmer; a cultivator or tiller of the ground; one who labors in tillage.

FLOURISH, v.i. To thrive; to grow luxuriantly; to increase and enlarge, as a healthy growing plant.

Key Scripture

Psalm 104:16 — "The trees of the LORD are full of sap; the cedars of Lebanon, which he hath planted;"

Psalm 104:14 — "He causeth the grass to grow for the cattle, and herb for the service of man: that he may bring forth food out of the earth;"

Psalm 1:3 — "And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper."

John 15:1 — "I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman."

Modern Corruption

Creation is treated either as raw material with no relation to God or as itself divine; Psalm 104 presents a world God actively tends, distinct from him and belonging to him.

expand to see more

Two opposite errors are live at once. The materialist account treats the natural world as resource — valuable in proportion to its use, with no owner above the user. The pantheist and neo-pagan account, which has been gaining ground for a generation, treats nature as itself sacred, and slides easily into the worship of the creature more than the Creator. Psalm 104 grants what is true in the second and denies its conclusion. The cedars are magnificent and full of life, and they are the trees of the LORD, planted by him. They are neither commodity nor deity; they are his property, and that is the ground of both their dignity and their limits.

The practical corollary is a doctrine of stewardship that owes nothing to either camp. A Christian cares for creation because it belongs to God and man was placed in the garden to dress it and to keep it, not because the earth is sacred and not merely because resources are scarce. And the figure has an inward application the Bible presses hardest. Sap is invisible; a tree full of it and a tree dying look similar from a distance and are distinguished by fruit in season and a leaf that does not wither. That is exactly the test Psalm 1 applies to a man, and the Lord applies to a branch: abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew saba (H7646), to be satisfied or filled; ets (H6086), a tree; erez (H730), a cedar; nata (H5193), to plant.

expand to see more

Hebrew saba (H7646) — to be satisfied, filled to the full; rendered full of sap.

Hebrew ets (H6086) — a tree, wood; the trees of the LORD.

Hebrew erez (H730) — a cedar; the great timber of Lebanon.

Hebrew nata (H5193) — to plant, to fix; the decisive clause, which he hath planted.

Greek georgos (G1092) — a husbandman, a tiller; the Father in John 15:1.

Usage

"“the trees of the LORD are full of sap” — life no man cultivated."

"“which he hath planted” — the clause that assigns ownership."

"“his leaf also shall not wither” — the same figure, of a man."
